readings.title: The Months
readings.challenge: Hear the year go round, one month at a time.
readings.focus: Each month brings its own weather, flowers, animals or treats, from January snow to Christmas in December.
readings.context: Sara Coleridge wrote this poem to help her son learn the months, and it became famous on its own. Dams are mother sheep; gilliflowers are sweet-smelling flowers; sheaves of corn are bundles of cut grain, and the harvest home is the end of harvest; a pheasant is a large bird; sportsmen here are hunters. These are English seasons, and your months may look different.

excerpt.locator: Pretty Lessons, “The Months,” the complete poem; opens “JANUARY brings the snow, Makes our feet and fingers glow.”; closes “Chill December brings the sleet, Blazing fire, and Christmas treat.”.

questions.prompt: What does January bring, and what does it do to our feet and fingers?
facilitatorNotes: Snow, which makes feet and fingers glow with cold.
evidence: JANUARY brings the snow,
Makes our feet and fingers glow.

questions.prompt: Which month brings lambs, and which brings roses?
facilitatorNotes: May brings lambs; June brings tulips, lilies and roses. Children can find their birthday month and hear what the poem gives it.
evidence: May brings flocks of pretty lambs,
June brings tulips, lilies, roses,

questions.prompt: Which month in the poem is most like this month where you live, and which is least like it?
facilitatorNotes: Answers depend on where the family lives; ask for the poem’s line and one difference. This helps children notice that a poem describes one place and its seasons.
evidence: Dull November brings the blast,
Chill December brings the sleet,

readings.title: The Suspicious Cock and Hen
readings.challenge: Follow how one unkind remark sets off a farmyard uproar.
readings.focus: The cock and hen accuse an innocent cat and so give her the very idea they feared.
readings.context: Suspicious means quick to think someone is up to no good. Intent means plan; in a trice means in an instant; dame means wife. Clacking, gobbling and quacking are farmyard noises, so make them as you read. The last verse gives the poem’s lesson.
readings.contentNote: The cat seizes a chick, and the old woman threatens to beat the noisy animals.

excerpt.locator: Pretty Lessons, “The Suspicious Cock and Hen,” the complete poem; opens “A COCK and a Hen Stepp’d out of their pen, And quickly beginning to chat, Said Cock to…”; closes “…return; And making a noise In birds, beasts, and boys, It is but a silly concern.”.

questions.prompt: What does the cock think the cat is up to?
facilitatorNotes: Prowling about to steal their chickens.
evidence: Pray look at that ugly old cat.
To steal our sweet Chickens away;

questions.prompt: What was the cat really doing, and what gave her the idea of taking a chick?
facilitatorNotes: She was only catching mice; the hen’s silly words put the idea of seizing a chick into her head.
evidence: But merely on catching of Mice;
First put in her head

questions.prompt: The poem says “ill-natured speech provokes an ill-natured return.” What does that mean in this story?
facilitatorNotes: The hen spoke unkindly to the cat, and the cat answered by doing the very thing she was accused of; then everyone’s noise made it worse. Children may say “be kind and kindness comes back”; ask whether the cat was right to grab the chick, since in the end she gives it up.
evidence: That ill-natured speech
Provokes an ill-natured return;

readings.title: The Nightingale
readings.challenge: Hear two different ideas about the same bird’s song.
readings.focus: Poets call the nightingale’s song sad, but this poem says she is merry, and sad only when she loses her nest.
readings.context: A nightingale is a small brown bird that comes to England in spring and sings at night. Poets called her Philomel, a name from an old sad story. To vow and to aver both mean to say firmly; her pipe is her song; keen regret is sharp sorrow. Storks and starlings are other birds.
readings.contentNote: The last verse speaks of boys robbing the bird’s nest.

excerpt.locator: Pretty Lessons, “The Nightingale,” the complete poem; opens “IN April comes the Nightingale, That sings when day’s departed; The poets call her…”; closes “…Stork or Starling; What mother would not weep and cry _To lose_ her precious darling.”.

facilitatorNotes: When the day has gone, at night. She comes in April.
evidence: That sings when day’s departed;

questions.prompt: What do the poets say about her song, and what does this poem say instead?
facilitatorNotes: The poets say she is broken-hearted and her song sounds like sorrow; this poem says she is merry, with a clear and thrilling song and no worries.
evidence: And vow she’s broken-hearted.
No, ’tis the merry Nightingale,

questions.prompt: When does the Nightingale really grieve? Do you think she is right to?
facilitatorNotes: When boys have robbed her nest, as any mother bird would. Children may say anyone would be sad to lose her babies; the poem asks the listener to be kind to nests.
evidence: She grieves when boys have robb’d her nest,
What mother would not weep and cry

readings.title: Signs of Rain
readings.challenge: Collect the clues that rain is coming.
readings.focus: Birds and animals all seem to know the weather is changing, each showing it in its own way.
readings.context: Long ago country people watched animals to guess the weather. A thrush is a songbird; to devour is to eat up. A hillock is a small hill; trooping means going in a group. Rooks are big black birds, like crows, that live together and chatter. Next time clouds gather, watch the birds together.

excerpt.locator: Pretty Lessons, “Signs of Rain,” the complete poem; opens “THE Thrush has been silent for many a long day, But now he sings loudly, and what does he…”; closes “…are discussing the very same matter— While homeward returning how loudly they chatter!”.

questions.prompt: Why is the Thrush singing loudly after being silent so long?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks a shower is coming, and after rain there will be worms and slugs for him to eat.
evidence: He says that he thinks there will soon be a shower,
And he shall have earth-worms and slugs to devour.

questions.prompt: Which other animals seem to know the weather is changing?
facilitatorNotes: The swan brushes the water with her wing, the woodpecker drums, the deer go up the little hill, the swallows dart about, and the rooks chatter.
evidence: The Woodpecker drums, though she lately was drooping;
The Swallows are darting and wheeling about,

questions.prompt: What are the Rooks talking about, the poem says? Could birds really know when rain is coming?
facilitatorNotes: The same thing as everyone else: the change in the weather. The poem imagines them discussing it. Birds do often behave differently before a storm, which is why people watched them; children can say what they have noticed.
evidence: The Rooks are discussing the very same matter—
While homeward returning how loudly they chatter!
